---
title: Your First Script
---

Many tasks need a few commands, not just one. If it is something you do more
than once, typing them all again each time gets tedious, and it is easy to get
one of them wrong.

A **shell script** solves that. It is a file with commands in it. The shell
reads the file and runs the commands one by one, just as if you typed them. Get
it right once, and you can run it any time.

In this chapter, we'll learn how to:

* write a script with a single command and run it
* write a script with several commands
* use comments to say what a script is for

And the one idea to hold on to from the start: **the shell reads a line from a
file just the way it reads a line you type.**

## An editor

Putting commands in a file needs a way to edit files. `nano` will do, and it
runs in the terminal so you do not have to go anywhere else. If you have not
set up an editor yet, see [Setting up Editor](../../setup/editor.qmd).

## A place to keep them

Scripts are files, and they will pile up. Let's give them a directory of their
own:

```session
$ cd
```

```session
$ mkdir scripts
```

```session
$ cd scripts
```

Everything in this section happens here.

## Hello, world

Open a new file:

```session
$ nano hello.sh
```

Type a single line into it, and save:

```{.bash filename="hello.sh"}
echo "Hello, world!"
```

That is the whole script. It is an ordinary text file, and `cat` will show it
to you like any other:

```session
$ cat hello.sh
echo "Hello, world!"
```

To run it, hand the file to `bash`:

```session
$ bash hello.sh
Hello, world!
```

`bash` is the shell itself - the same program that has been reading your typed
lines all along. Given a file name, it reads the lines in that file instead of
the ones you type. There is nothing else to it.

The name ends in `.sh` by custom, so that a directory listing tells you what
the file is. Nothing depends on it. `bash hello` would work just as well if the
file were called `hello`.

## More than one command

A script is not limited to one line. Make a second file:

```{.bash filename="numbers.sh"}
echo "Counting to five:"
seq 5
echo "Done."
```

```session
$ bash numbers.sh
Counting to five:
1
2
3
4
5
Done.
```

Top to bottom, one command at a time, each one finishing before the next
starts. That is exactly what happens when you type three lines by hand.

## Saying what it is for

A line beginning with `#` is a **comment**. The shell ignores it. Comments are
there for the person reading the file - which, more often than not, is you, six
months later, wondering what this thing was for.

Here is a script worth keeping: a pipeline that prints the date in big letters.

```{.bash filename="figdate.sh"}
#
# Prints the date in big letters.
#

date | figlet
```

```session
$ bash figdate.sh
__        __       _   ____                 ___
\ \      / /__  __| | / ___|  ___ _ __     / _ \
 \ \ /\ / / _ \/ _` | \___ \ / _ \ '_ \   | (_) |
  \ V  V /  __/ (_| |  ___) |  __/ |_) |   \__, |
   \_/\_/ \___|\__,_| |____/ \___| .__/      /_/
                                 |_|
 _  ___    _ ____    _  _  _____   ___ ____ _____   ____   ___ ____   __
/ |/ _ \ _/ |___ \ _| || ||___ /  |_ _/ ___|_   _| |___ \ / _ \___ \ / /_
| | | | (_) | __) (_) || |_ |_ \   | |\___ \ | |     __) | | | |__) | '_ \
| | |_| |_| |/ __/ _|__   _|__) |  | | ___) || |    / __/| |_| / __/| (_) |
|_|\___/(_)_|_____(_)  |_||____/  |___|____/ |_|   |_____|\___/_____|\___/
```

Notice what went into the file: a pipe. Wildcards, quotes and the `$` forms all
work in a script too, and for the same reason - the shell reads a line from a
file exactly the way it reads a line you type. Nothing you have learned so far
stops working when you put it in a file.

## Summary

| What you write | What it means |
|----------------|---------------|
| `nano hello.sh` | opens `hello.sh` in an editor, creating it if it is new |
| `bash hello.sh` | runs the commands in `hello.sh`, top to bottom |
| `# ...` | a comment - the shell ignores the rest of the line |
| `.sh` | the customary ending for a script's name; nothing depends on it |

And the one idea to carry forward: a script is a file of commands, and running
it is the same as typing them.
